golden.evidence: The PR description promises a shared single-thread executor to serialize pull/push operations, but the actual code still uses `kotlin.concurrent.thread` for all four entry points. Each invocation spawns a fresh, unconstrained thread. Concurrent pulls and pushes remain fully possible on rapid key presses or menu clicks, leaving the interleaved repository read/write problem the PR claims to fix entirely unsolved.

`localRepository` is declared as `var localRepository: LocalRepository? = null` (nullable). Inside the non-inline `uiRun` lambda, it is passed directly to `localRepositoryToProject(localRepository: LocalRepository)` which requires a non-null type. Kotlin's smart-cast rules do not apply to captured `var` variables inside non-inline lambdas, so this is either a compile error under the K2 compiler or will throw a NullPointerException at runtime if the smart-cast is somehow accepted. The fix is to capture a non-nullable local copy before the lambda: `val repo = localRepository!!; uiRun { localRepositoryToProject(repo) }`.

`uiRun` delegates to `SwingUtilities.invokeLater` (asynchronous). Scheduling `localRepositoryToProject` inside `uiRun` means `pull()` returns — and the background thread exits — before the project state has actually been updated. If a new pull is triggered immediately afterwards (which is possible because no serialization exists), `projectToLocalRepository` in the new pull reads stale project renames/comments from before the previous pull's EDT update ran. The same problem applies to the equivalent block at the end of `push()` (lines 645–648).

In `push()`, `projectToLocalRepository(localRepository)` is called on the background thread at the top of the retry loop, reading `codeData.renames/comments`. However, the previous iteration's `writeRemoteRepository` and script have already updated the remote, and any pending `localRepositoryToProject` from a previous pull (dispatched asynchronously to the EDT) may not have run yet. This makes the `localRepository` snapshot built from project state inconsistent with what was last pushed to the remote, potentially re-introducing already-resolved renames into the next write.

ignored.evidence: `projectToLocalRepository` (and its callee `getProjectRenames`/`getProjectComments`) reads `context!!.args.codeData.renames` and `.comments` directly on the background thread. `localRepositoryToProject` (dispatched to the EDT via `uiRun`) writes those same fields via `setProjectRenames`/`setProjectComments`. Since multiple background threads can exist simultaneously (finding #1 — no serialization), concurrent reads on a background thread and writes on the EDT to these unsynchronized mutable fields constitute a data race.

`showError` (and `showInfo`) dispatch dialogs asynchronously via `invokeLater`. The background thread returns immediately after scheduling the error dialog, so a subsequent pull or push can start (and potentially show its own error) before the first dialog has even appeared on screen. This causes out-of-order dialogs and means the user may see an error for an operation they no longer regard as current. Previously, `JOptionPane.showMessageDialog` was blocking; the new async dispatch removes that back-pressure without any replacement synchronisation point.

`PluginMockery.pull` and `push` are still populated with the `{ kotlin.concurrent.thread { this.pull() } }` menu-action lambdas, but no test calls them any more — tests now invoke `plugin.pull()` / `plugin.push()` directly. Consequently, the tests never exercise the actual menu-triggered code path (which spawns a background thread), so any threading defect in that path, including the missing serialization, goes completely untested.

`kotlin.concurrent.thread` creates non-daemon threads by default, so a long-running script or blocked conflict dialog can keep the JVM alive after the UI is closed. The background worker should be daemonized or shut down explicitly to avoid shutdown stalls.

These shortcut handlers also create non-daemon threads via `kotlin.concurrent.thread`, so a blocked pull/push triggered from the keyboard can prevent JVM shutdown. Use a daemon executor thread or ensure the worker is shut down with the plugin lifecycle.
